book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

clue.text: Persian emperor's rewritten chapter on coke

definitions.note: The definition is a possessive with its noun left out: what is the Persian emperor's, and what the answer names, is the seat he sits on.

indicators.note: A chapter that has been rewritten holds the same material in a new arrangement, which is what happens to the letters standing after it.

parts.note: thirteen letters to be set down in another order, which is the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: An emperor has gone back over the chapter he wrote about coke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coke' reads as the drug or the drink and is four of the thirteen letters. The throne was the Mughal emperors' jewelled seat, carried off to Persia in 1739 and a byword for the Iranian monarchy ever since.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peacock Throne is the seat of the Persian shahs, so the thing that is the Persian emperor's, and the byword for his rule, is this.

clue.text: Considers points for two lots of wise men?

parts.note: east and north are two of the compass points, and it is their initials that are wanted
wise men arrive three at a time, so two lots of them make six, and six in Roman figures is VI
a sage is a wise man, and the plural follows the plural in the clue

explanation.surface: Somebody is working out the points to award two parties of wise men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' looks like a score being handed out and is the compass. The wise men who come in threes are the Magi of the Christmas story, which is the sum the question mark is covering.
explanation.definitionFit: To envisage a plan is to form a picture of it and turn it over, which is what it is to consider one.

clue.text: Bring converse of train to road shortly

parts.note: the converse of train to road is car to rail: a car is the road counterpart of a train
under the same swap road becomes railway, abbreviated RY

explanation.surface: A transport planner wants to switch trains for road traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the pairing: train to road becomes car to railway, giving CAR then RY.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry something is to convey it, to bring it along.

clue.text: Carbon also used for burning

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon

indicators.note: used in the sense of worn and knocked about, so the letters of also are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Carbon, too, is put to use as fuel on the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description: coals are lumps of carbon used for burning. 'used' rearranges ALSO into OALS after the C.
explanation.definitionFit: Coals are pieces of coal or charcoal, which are mostly carbon and are burnt as fuel.

clue.text: Mock exam: what's litmus?

definitions.meaning: read as a school's practice run, printed and handed out a term before the real thing
read again as chemistry: the dye that goes red in acid and blue in alkali, sold soaked into little strips for dipping

explanation.surface: In the middle of a practice exam somebody asks what litmus actually is.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are paper that something is done with: one is printed with questions, the other steeped in dye. The hyphen in the enumeration is the only sign that two words are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A test paper is the sheet of questions a mock exam consists of, and litmus paper is the chemist's strip for testing acidity: the same two words in two trades.

clue.text: Pretty girl goes bottom first into circle, refusing to comply

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the altered girl sits within the circle word

parts.note: a ring is a circle

indicators.note: in a down answer the bottom is the last letter, so it moves to the front

parts.note: a belle is a beautiful girl or woman

explanation.surface: A pretty girl slides bottom first into a ring, disobeying her instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes bottom first' moves the last E of BELLE to the front to make EBELL, which goes 'into' RING.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebelling is resisting authority, so someone rebelling is declining to obey or conform.

clue.text: Horse's refusal, say?

definitions.note: The definition is a possessive with its noun dropped — the horse's own noise — and the question mark is the licence the setter takes for it.

indicators.note: To say a thing is to make its sound, so what matters about the word in front is how it comes out of the mouth, not how it is spelt.

parts.note: a refusal is a nay, the vote against a motion in its older spelling

explanation.surface: A horse refusing, at a fence perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: A horse that stops dead at a fence is said to refuse, and the clue lets it announce the fact out loud. 'Nay' is the parliamentary no, the opposite of aye.
explanation.definitionFit: A neigh is the cry a horse makes, so the possessive with its noun left off points straight at the animal's own noise.

clue.text: China Waller turns up with cars to rent

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up means the name is written bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: Fats Waller was an American jazz pianist and composer
Fords are cars made by the Ford Motor Company
to hire something is to rent it

explanation.surface: A man called Waller arrives with china and cars for hire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country but porcelain. 'turns up' reverses FATS, Fats Waller's nickname, to give STAF.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffordshire is the English county of the Potteries, and its name is used for the china and ceramics made there.

clue.text: Corn goddess keeps a lot of sticks on circle for measuring slow-down

definitions.note: describes an instrument, a noun, by its purpose

indicators.note: the goddess keeps, or holds inside her, the other letters

parts.note: Demeter is the Greek goddess of corn and harvest

indicators.note: in this down entry, on means the shortened sticks sit on top of the circle
a lot of means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: celery comes in sticks
O is a circle

explanation.surface: The harvest goddess stores a pile of sticks on a ring to gauge braking.
explanation.definitionFit: A decelerometer is an instrument that records deceleration, for example when testing vehicle brakes.

clue.text: Acknowledgement about greeting to sailors in pub (Greek)

indicators.note: What goes about a thing goes round it, so the word in front splits and stands on either side of everything that follows.

parts.note: ta is the everyday British thank-you, and it parts to take the rest between its two letters
ave is the Latin hail, the greeting Romans wrote and Catholics still sing
the Royal Navy shortens to RN, and its men are the sailors meant

explanation.surface: A word of thanks and a greeting to the sailors drinking in a Greek bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is the setter naming a language rather than translating anything. 'Acknowledgement' is the thank-you sense, not a receipt, and it is the smallest of the three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A taverna is the Greek version of the local, a small restaurant and bar, which is what the bracketed language is there to pin down.

clue.text: Ottoman emperor's vehicle returned with two drinks (English)

definitions.note: the clue's possessive stands for the emperor's court or government, which is what the answer names

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the vehicle word is read backwards

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle
lime, as in lime juice, and port are both drinks

explanation.surface: A sultan's carriage comes back carrying a couple of drinks for an Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns BUS into SUB. The Sublime Porte was the name for the Ottoman government at Constantinople, from the gate of the Grand Vizier's palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sublime Porte was the court and central government of the Ottoman Empire, the sultan's seat of power.

clue.text: Suspicious, if perhaps reserved

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of if may be arranged another way

parts.note: someone shy is reserved

explanation.surface: Being withdrawn can make a person look shifty, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IF into FI, which comes before SHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishy is an informal word for doubtful or arousing suspicion, as in a fishy story.

clue.text: See about a lot of beauty in tomb

indicators.note: What is about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word in front splits and the rest is set between its halves.
A lot of a word is most of it and not the whole, so what follows arrives with its tail cut off.

parts.note: the clue's own word taken at face value, opened up to hold what comes next
pulchritude is the formal word for beauty, and the instruction in front keeps most of it

explanation.surface: Somebody is being shown a good deal of the beauty inside a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: Pulchritude is a Latinate word for good looks that survives mainly in jokes and crosswords, and it does all the work here. The Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem is the tomb the answer is best known for.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepulchre is a tomb cut in rock or built of stone, the word the Bible uses for the one Christ was laid in.

clue.text: Paper instrument for a body

definitions.meaning: read as newsprint: the journal a party or a union puts out to speak for it
read again as anatomy: the Greek word behind it means a tool, and a body's working parts are its tools

explanation.surface: An instrument made of paper, supplied to a body of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Three senses sit in five words: the party's journal, the pipes in the church loft, and the liver or the lungs. Only two of them are being defined, and the church is there for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's paper is called its organ, the thing it speaks through; and an organ of a body is one of its instruments, from the Greek word for tool.

clue.text: Where you needn't 3 4 sounds 11 in 8

definitions.note: The definition is a cross-reference rather than a synonym: 8's answer is the county the place stands in, which is the clue's way of saying which of the two Newcastles is wanted.

parts.note: 3 and 4 spell out the errand of the proverb: taking coal to the town that dug it is the byword for a pointless journey

indicators.note: 'Sounds' asks for what a word comes out as when it is spoken rather than how it is spelt, so the piece after it is written the way the ear takes it.

parts.note: 11's answer is the word said aloud here, and sub is Latin for under

explanation.walkthrough: Coals to Newcastle is the proverb for a wasted errand, and its Newcastle is the one on the Tyne; the joke is that this is the other one, a market town in the Potteries. Lyme was the forest it stood under.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle-under-Lyme is a Staffordshire town, so the county 8 spells out is what the clue offers in place of a definition, fixing which Newcastle to write.

clue.text: Large size of dial put me off

indicators.note: Something that has gone off is no longer as it should be, so the letters standing in front of it are not in the order they should be either.

parts.note: nine letters to be set down in another order, which is the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: The sheer size of the dial was enough to put me off.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words that sound like a complaint about the dial are the material the clue works on. Physics borrowed the answer later for the height of a wave above its resting line.
explanation.definitionFit: Amplitude is the noun for being ample — roominess, generous extent — so 'large size' is its plain meaning underneath the scientific one.

clue.text: She writes for the Thunderer and uses a disguise outside

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go outside, wrapping round the god
to disguise something is to change its appearance, so the letters of uses a are rearranged

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A woman writing for The Times, nicknamed the Thunderer, goes about in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thunderer is the old nickname of The Times, which suggests journalism, but here it is the god THOR. 'disguise' rearranges USES A into AUESS, and THOR goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An authoress is a female author, a woman who writes books or articles.

clue.text: See 15
Washing-up liquid isn't fit to drink

definitions.meaning: read as the bottle of detergent standing by the sink, and meant as the liquid you are left with once the plates are done
grey, greasy and going cold in the bowl — and the byword for tea that has been made far too weak

explanation.surface: A warning that the stuff in the bottle by the sink is not for drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is that washing-up liquid names a product in every British kitchen. The clue means its three words literally, and what they describe is the bowlful, not the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishwater is what stands in the bowl when the washing-up is over, and its name is proverbial for anything too weak and greasy to swallow.

clue.text: Go without commercials? You surprise me!

indicators.note: 'Without' in its older sense means outside, so the word in front stands round what follows instead of losing it.

parts.note: the clue's own word, parted so that it stands on either side of the rest
the commercials between television programmes are ads

explanation.surface: Watching something that carries no advertisements at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old preposition, the one in the hymn's green hill far away without a city wall: outside, not lacking. Gadso is a seventeenth-century oath, a politer stand-in for something stronger.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadso is an old exclamation of surprise or vexation, a softened oath, so it is what a speaker of the day said where we would say 'you surprise me!'

clue.text: Prince on river with fool has some bread

parts.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V, drinking his way through the taverns before he takes the crown
the Fal is the Cornish river that Falmouth stands at the mouth of
an oaf is a lumbering fool

explanation.surface: A prince beside a river with a fool, and some bread between them.
explanation.walkthrough: A prince and a fool in the same sentence is the Falstaff picture, which is what holds the surface together. Half a loaf is better than no bread is the proverb standing behind the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Half a loaf is literally part of a loaf — some bread rather than none — and the phrase lives on in the proverb about settling for it.

clue.text: Queen of Californian city's not broad in the beam

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it: the thing is a beam, and what the clue says about it is that it is a very narrow one.

indicators.note: 'Queen of the city's' is the double genitive of ordinary speech — the city's queen — so the city and its apostrophe-s are written first and the queen comes after.

parts.note: Los Angeles shortens to LA, and the clue's own apostrophe-s follows it
ER is the Queen's cipher, Elizabeth Regina, stamped on British post boxes

explanation.surface: A beauty queen from a Californian city who is not wide across the hips.
explanation.walkthrough: Broad in the beam is a ship's width carried over to a person's hips, and the answer is a beam of quite another kind. Los Angeles is the Californian city every crossword means.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser is a beam of light so narrow it stays a pencil over miles, which is what 'not broad in the beam' is claiming of it.

clue.text: French for good could be scarlet

definitions.note: The definition does not name a kind of scarlet: it points at the pair of words the answer completes, the childhood illness whose rash supplies the colour.

parts.note: F is the standard short form of French
what has gone for good has gone for ever, and it is the second word of that phrase that is wanted

explanation.surface: The French word for 'good' might turn out to be a shade of red.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers 'the French for good', as though a translation were being asked for, and the clue means its two halves separately. Scarlet fever takes its name from the rash that comes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlet fever is the childhood illness the colour word belongs to, so what 'scarlet' turns out to be short for is the answer.

clue.text: See 11
Fear makes father less than agreeable

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: less than the whole word means it falls short by its last letter

parts.note: nice means pleasant or agreeable

explanation.surface: Dad is in a mood that is not altogether pleasant, which frightens people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less than' agreeable means not quite NICE, so its final E goes to leave NIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Panic is sudden overwhelming fear or alarm.

clue.text: Badge put in parrot fashion

indicators.note: What is put in something goes inside it, so the word before it is written between the halves of the words after it.

parts.note: learning something parrot fashion is learning it by rote, and those four letters part to take the rest inside
to put a thing down is to set it down

explanation.surface: A badge pinned on in the manner of a parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: Parrot fashion is how a child learns a times table: by repetition, with no understanding of it at all. The badge is the ribbon a candidate wears at an election count.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosette is the ribbon badge pinned on at an election or a horse show, which is the sense of badge the clue wants.

clue.text: Brown beard in front trench

definitions.note: Two senses stand side by side rather than one: Vandyke brown is a pigment and a Vandyke is a beard, so the definition is not describing a beard that happens to be brown.

parts.note: the van is the front — the vanguard of an army is its leading part
a dyke is a ditch cut into the ground, the trench that drains a field

explanation.surface: A brown beard seen in the front trench.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Van Dyck painted Charles I and his court wearing the neat pointed beard that took his name, and the dark brown of those canvases took it too. The trenches are the surface's own idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Vandyke brown is the dark pigment named after the painter, and a Vandyke is the trim pointed beard he gave his sitters: two separate senses of one word.

clue.text: Smile about ruse in changing fees? I'm too sad to

definitions.note: the definition completes itself with the clue's first word: I'm too sad to smile, which describes someone deeply sorrowful

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the smile word goes round everything else

parts.note: a grin is a broad smile

indicators.note: in places the ruse inside the rearranged fees
changing means altering, so the letters of fees are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a trick is a ruse or deception

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to smile about a con involving altered charges but says they are too unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges FEES into EFSE, TRICK goes 'in' after EFS, and GRIN goes 'about' the lot. The definition borrows 'Smile' from the start: someone too sad to smile.
explanation.definitionFit: Grief-stricken describes someone overwhelmed by sorrow, so unhappy they cannot raise a smile.
